sentences.text: Lewisuchus was a small archosaur, a group of reptiles closely related to dinosaurs, that measured about one meter in length.
Its back was protected by osteoderms, which are bony plates embedded in the skin that functioned as armor.
A specimen found in 2013 and described in 2019 offered key evidence suggesting two previously distinct genera were actually the same species.

Remains were first uncovered during a 1964–1965 expedition by the Museo de La Plata and Harvard's Museum of Comparative Zoology. Alfred Romer named the genus in 1972 after Arnold D. Lewis, the preparator who found the holotype skeleton.
Modern classification places Lewisuchus within the family Silesauridae.
Some researchers proposed that Pseudolagosuchus major and Lewisuchus admixtus are identical, representing basal members of this family.
This animal lived between 241.464 and 233.6 million years ago, spanning the Ladinian to Carnian stages, in the Chañares Formation of Argentina.
However, a 2014 study argued against merging Pseudolagosuchus major with Lewisuchus admixtus because the available fossil data did not overlap sufficiently to confirm they were the same creature.
